title: Design a Web Crawler
summary: End-to-end walkthrough: crawl 1B pages in 5 days with a host-sharded polite frontier, cached robots.txt and DNS, Bloom-filter and SimHash dedupe, and checkpointed recovery.
body:
## Practice first

Design a web crawler that starts from a set of seed URLs, downloads pages, extracts links and keeps going until it has fetched about 1 billion pages. The output is the raw HTML of every page, stored for a downstream indexing or ML-training pipeline. The crawler must be a good citizen of the web: it obeys robots.txt and never hammers a single site.

Spend about 10 minutes sketching before you read on: requirements, the main loop, what sits between "URL discovered" and "page stored", and the one number that sizes the fleet. Then compare. The interesting parts of this problem are not the fetch itself but scheduling (politeness), deduplication and surviving crashes in a job that runs for days.

## Functional requirements

Core (the system should be able to):

1. **Crawl from seeds:** take a list of seed URLs and fetch pages over HTTP(S).
2. **Discover and schedule:** extract links from fetched HTML, normalise them and schedule new URLs for fetching.
3. **Store content:** persist the raw page content and fetch metadata (status, headers, timestamp, content hash) for downstream consumers.

Out of scope: building the search index, ranking, rendering JavaScript-heavy pages in a headless browser, recrawl freshness policy beyond a sketch, and non-HTML media. Mention them, then park them.

## Non-functional requirements

- **Scale and deadline:** 1 billion pages in 5 days. This throughput target drives fleet size more than anything else.
- **Politeness:** at most one in-flight request per host and a minimum delay between requests to the same host (default 1 second, longer if the site is slow or asks for it). robots.txt rules are honoured for every fetch.
- **Fault tolerance:** a worker or node crash loses at most a few seconds of progress; the crawl resumes from durable state rather than restarting. Crawl state favours durability and availability over strict consistency: fetching a page twice is a small waste, losing the frontier is a disaster.
- **Efficiency:** avoid re-fetching the same URL and avoid storing near-identical content (mirrors, session-ID variants, boilerplate pages).
- **Robustness:** survive spider traps, malformed HTML, enormous responses and hosts that never respond.

## Back-of-the-envelope

Only the numbers that change a decision:

- **Throughput:** 5 days is 432,000 s, so 10^9 / 432,000 ≈ **2,300 pages/s** sustained. Plan for about 3,500/s to absorb retries, slow hosts and restarts.
- **Fetch concurrency:** a typical fetch takes about 1 s end to end (DNS, TCP+TLS, transfer). Little's law: 3,500 pages/s × 1 s ≈ **3,500 concurrent connections**. That is I/O-bound work, so a few dozen machines running async I/O (a few hundred connections each) suffice. Fetching is not the hard part.
- **Bandwidth:** with a median HTML page of about 100 KB, 3,500 × 100 KB ≈ 350 MB/s ≈ **2.8 Gbps** ingress, spread over the fleet. Fine, but it rules out a single-box design.
- **Storage:** 10^9 × 100 KB = **100 TB** raw, about 25 TB if compressed 4:1. That belongs in a blob store, not a database.
- **Politeness ceiling:** at 1 request/s per host, sustaining 2,300 pages/s needs at least 2,300 hosts active at any time. Large sites cap out: a single host can contribute at most 432,000 pages in 5 days. So the scheduler must keep many thousands of hosts in rotation, which is why the frontier is organised by host.
- **URL-seen set:** link extraction typically discovers 5 to 10 times more URLs than you fetch, say 10 billion. Storing 16-byte hashes exactly is 160 GB; a Bloom filter at 1% false positives needs about 9.6 bits per element, roughly **12 GB**. That fits in memory when sharded, which is the reason to use one.

## Core entities

- **URL record:** normalised URL, host, URL hash, priority, depth, discovered-from, status (queued, fetched, failed, skipped), next-eligible time.
- **Host record:** host name, cached robots.txt rules and expiry, crawl delay, resolved IPs with TTL, error count, page budget used.
- **Page:** URL hash, fetch time, HTTP status, headers, content hash (exact), SimHash (near-duplicate fingerprint), blob key of the stored body.
- **Crawl job:** seeds, scope rules (domains, max depth), deadlines and limits.

```mermaid
erDiagram
    HOST ||--o{ URL : contains
    URL ||--o| PAGE : "fetched as"
    CRAWL_JOB ||--o{ URL : schedules
    HOST {
        string host
        string robots_rules
        int crawl_delay_ms
        string resolved_ip
    }
    URL {
        string url_hash
        string url
        int priority
        int depth
        string status
    }
    PAGE {
        string url_hash
        int http_status
        string content_sha256
        string simhash
        string blob_key
    }
```

A host owns many URLs; a URL that has been fetched has at most one current page version; a crawl job scopes which URLs are eligible. The host record is where politeness and DNS state live, which matters for the deep dives.

## API

A crawler is mostly a batch system, so the "API" is a small control plane used by operators and downstream consumers rather than end users. All endpoints require service authentication.

```http
POST /v1/crawls
{ "seeds": ["https://example.org/"], "scope": {"allowedDomains": ["example.org"], "maxDepth": 12}, "maxPages": 1000000000 }
-> 201 { "crawlId": "c_81" }

GET /v1/crawls/c_81
-> 200 { "status": "running", "fetched": 412000000, "queued": 2900000000, "pagesPerSecond": 2410, "errorRate": 0.031 }

POST /v1/crawls/c_81/pause      -> 202
POST /v1/crawls/c_81/resume     -> 202

GET /v1/crawls/c_81/pages?since=2026-10-29T00:00:00Z&cursor=...
-> 200 { "items": [{ "url": "...", "blobKey": "...", "contentHash": "..." }], "nextCursor": "..." }
```

The pages feed is cursor-paginated so an indexer can stream results incrementally. In practice the indexer may instead consume a "page stored" event stream; both are fine to mention.

## High-level design

Build it one requirement at a time.

**Crawl from seeds.** Seeds go into a **URL frontier**, the queue of URLs waiting to be fetched. **Fetcher workers** pull a URL, resolve the host through a **DNS cache**, check **robots.txt** rules, and download the page with strict timeouts and a size cap.

**Store content.** The fetcher writes the raw body to a **blob store** (object storage) under a key derived from the URL hash and fetch time, and writes a small metadata row to a **metadata store** (a wide-column or key-value store keyed by URL hash).

**Discover and schedule.** A separate **parser** stage reads stored pages, extracts and normalises links, filters them through **URL dedupe** (a Bloom filter backed by the metadata store) and scope rules, and pushes survivors back into the frontier. Content fingerprints are checked by **content dedupe** before the page is marked as useful.

Separating fetch from parse with a durable queue matters: fetchers are network-bound, parsers are CPU-bound, and they scale independently. A parser bug does not stall downloads, and pages can be re-parsed later without re-fetching.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Seeds["Seed URLs"] --> F[["URL frontier"]]
    F --> W["Fetcher workers"]
    W --> DNS[("DNS cache")]
    W --> R[("robots.txt cache")]
    W --> Web["Websites"]
    W --> B[("Blob store")]
    W --> M[("Metadata store")]
    W --> PQ[["Parse queue"]]
    PQ --> P["Parser workers"]
    P --> CD["Content dedupe"]
    P --> UD["URL dedupe (Bloom filter)"]
    UD --> F
```

Walk one URL through it: the frontier hands `https://example.org/a` to a fetcher only when `example.org` is eligible under politeness. The fetcher resolves the host from the DNS cache, checks the cached robots rules, downloads up to a 10 MB cap with a 30 s total timeout, stores the body in the blob store, writes metadata, and publishes "fetched url_hash X" to the parse queue. A parser loads the body, computes the content hash and SimHash, extracts 60 links, normalises them, drops the 50 already seen, and enqueues 10 new URLs into the frontier.

## Deep dives

### 1. The frontier: politeness without starving throughput

**Problem.** A plain FIFO queue fails both politeness and throughput. Pages link heavily within their own site, so the queue fills with long runs of the same host. Either workers hammer that host, or they sit idle waiting for its delay to expire while thousands of other hosts are ready.

**Bad: one global queue plus a "last fetched" check.** Workers pop a URL, see the host was hit 200 ms ago, and push it back. Most pops become re-queues, the queue churns and throughput collapses.

**Good: a queue per host.** Keep one FIFO per host and a scheduler that picks hosts round-robin. Politeness becomes structural. But priority is lost (an important page waits behind 50,000 unimportant ones on the same host), and millions of mostly-idle per-host queues are expensive to scan.

**Great: two-tier frontier (front queues for priority, back queues for politeness).** This is the classic Mercator design. URLs enter one of a few **front queues** by priority (for example, by estimated page importance or depth). A router moves URLs from front queues into a bounded set of **back queues**, each holding URLs for exactly one host at a time. A **min-heap** keyed by "next time this host may be fetched" tells workers which back queue is ready. After each fetch the host's next-eligible time is set to now plus max(crawl delay, k × last response time), so slow hosts are automatically treated more gently.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    In["New URLs"] --> Pri["Prioritiser"]
    Pri --> FQ1[["Front queue: high"]]
    Pri --> FQ2[["Front queue: medium"]]
    Pri --> FQ3[["Front queue: low"]]
    FQ1 --> Router["Back-queue router (biased pick)"]
    FQ2 --> Router
    FQ3 --> Router
    Router --> BQ1[["Back queue: host A"]]
    Router --> BQ2[["Back queue: host B"]]
    Router --> BQ3[["Back queue: host C"]]
    Heap["Min-heap: host to next eligible time"] --> Fetch["Fetcher picks ready host"]
    BQ1 --> Fetch
    BQ2 --> Fetch
    BQ3 --> Fetch
```

The prioritiser decides what matters; the back queues and heap decide when it is polite to fetch it. A good rule of thumb is about three back queues per fetcher thread so a ready host is almost always available.

**Distribution.** The frontier is too big for one machine (billions of URLs), so shard it **by host**: hash the registered domain to a frontier shard with consistent hashing. Every URL for a host lands on the same shard, so politeness is enforced locally with no cross-node coordination. When a parser discovers a URL for a host owned by another shard, it forwards it there. Each shard spills its queues to local disk (or an embedded store like RocksDB) and keeps only the queue heads in memory.

### 2. robots.txt and DNS: caching the per-host work

**Problem.** Every fetch needs a robots.txt decision and a DNS resolution. Doing both from scratch on each of 2,300 fetches/s would triple the request count to target sites and swamp resolvers, which are often the hidden bottleneck in crawlers.

**robots.txt.** Fetch `/robots.txt` once per host (scheme plus host plus port), parse it and cache the rules on the host record. RFC 9309 says crawlers should not use a cached copy for more than 24 hours unless the file is unreachable, so a 24-hour TTL is a sensible default. Handle the edge cases explicitly: a 4xx on robots.txt generally means "no restrictions", while a 5xx or network failure should be treated as "disallow everything" for that host until a retry succeeds. `Crawl-delay` is not part of the RFC, but many crawlers honour it as a hint for the minimum delay.

**DNS.** Run a local caching resolver on each fetcher node (or a shared resolver tier), respect record TTLs with a floor of a few minutes, and pre-resolve hosts when URLs enter their back queue so the lookup is off the fetch's critical path. Because frontier shards own hosts, the DNS cache hit rate on each shard is high. Also use the resolved IP for politeness in addition to the host name: thousands of small sites on one shared-hosting IP should not each get their own 1 req/s budget.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant FQ as Frontier shard
    participant W as Fetcher
    participant D as DNS cache
    participant R as Robots cache
    participant S as Website
    FQ->>W: next URL for ready host
    W->>D: resolve host
    D-->>W: IP (cached, TTL ok)
    W->>R: rules for host
    alt rules missing or older than 24h
        W->>S: GET /robots.txt
        S-->>W: rules
        W->>R: store rules
    end
    W->>W: path allowed?
    W->>S: GET page (timeout, size cap)
    S-->>W: 200 HTML
    W->>FQ: host next eligible = now + delay
```

The two caches turn per-fetch overhead into per-host overhead. The final step is what keeps the heap honest: the fetcher reports back so the host is not scheduled again until its delay elapses.

### 3. Deduplication: URLs and content

**URL dedupe.** First normalise: lowercase scheme and host, drop default ports and fragments, resolve relative paths, sort or strip known tracking parameters (`utm_*`, session IDs), and apply a length cap. Then check "have we seen this?".

- **Bad:** query the metadata store for every extracted link. At 10 links per page that is 23,000+ point reads/s just to discard mostly-known URLs.
- **Good:** an exact in-memory hash set. Correct, but 10 billion entries is 160 GB of hashes before overhead.
- **Great:** a **Bloom filter** per frontier shard (sharded by host, like the frontier), about 12 GB in total for 10 billion URLs at 1% false positives. A negative answer is definitive, so most new URLs skip the database entirely. A positive answer is either "seen" or a 1% false positive. Accept that 1% of genuinely new URLs are skipped (a deliberate trade for a crawl of this size), or confirm positives against the metadata store if completeness matters more. Persist the filter with each checkpoint.

**Content dedupe.** Different URLs often serve the same content: `http` and `https` variants, mirrors, printer-friendly pages, session IDs in paths.

- **Exact duplicates:** SHA-256 of the normalised body, stored in a key-value index. A hit means "do not store again; record an alias to the existing blob".
- **Near duplicates:** pages that differ only by a timestamp or an ad block have different hashes. **SimHash** produces a 64-bit fingerprint where similar documents differ in few bits; Google's crawler work treated fingerprints within a Hamming distance of 3 as near-duplicates. Finding all fingerprints within distance 3 is done by splitting the 64 bits into blocks and indexing permuted tables, so each lookup touches only a few candidates.

The recommendation is both: exact hashing is cheap and catches the majority; SimHash is applied where duplicate content is expensive (storage, training-data quality). Do dedupe in the parser stage, off the fetch path.

### 4. Fault tolerance over a five-day run

**Problem.** Over five days, machines will die, deploys will happen and some hosts will hang forever. The crawl must resume quickly and not restart from seeds.

**Bad: in-memory frontier.** A crash loses billions of queued URLs.

**Good: put everything in a managed queue (SQS, Kafka).** Durable, but a single queue cannot express per-host scheduling, and Kafka partitions cannot be reordered by next-eligible time.

**Great: host-sharded frontier with durable, checkpointed state, plus at-least-once pipeline stages.** Each frontier shard writes its queues to local disk with a write-ahead log and periodically checkpoints the queue heads, host heap and Bloom filter to the blob store. Shard ownership is held as a lease in a coordination service (etcd, ZooKeeper); if a node dies, another takes the lease and restores from the latest checkpoint plus log. The fetch-to-parse handoff uses a durable queue (Kafka or SQS) with at-least-once delivery. Because blob keys and metadata rows are keyed by URL hash, a replay after a crash simply overwrites with the same content: idempotent by construction.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Coord[("Lease store (etcd)")] --> S1["Frontier shard 1"]
    Coord --> S2["Frontier shard 2"]
    S1 --> WAL1[("Local WAL + queues")]
    S2 --> WAL2[("Local WAL + queues")]
    S1 -->|"checkpoint every 5 min"| CP[("Checkpoints in blob store")]
    S2 -->|"checkpoint every 5 min"| CP
    S1 --> W["Fetchers"]
    S2 --> W
    W --> PQ[["Parse queue (at least once)"]]
    CP -.->|"restore on failover"| S3["Replacement shard"]
```

Leases make ownership exclusive so two shards never schedule the same host (which would double its request rate). Checkpoints bound recovery work, and idempotent writes make replayed work harmless.

**Robustness against bad hosts and traps.** Use per-request connect and total timeouts (5 s and 30 s), a response size cap, a per-host page budget, a maximum URL depth and length, and heuristics for traps such as calendars that generate infinite "next month" links or repeating path segments (`/a/b/a/b/a/b`). Hosts with a high error rate get exponential back-off and eventually a cool-down period, freeing capacity for healthy ones.

### 5. Scaling to the deadline

Fleet size falls out of the numbers. About 3,500 concurrent fetches at a few hundred connections per node is roughly 15 to 20 fetcher nodes with headroom. Parsing is CPU-bound: if parsing and fingerprinting a page costs about 10 ms of CPU, 3,500 pages/s needs about 35 cores, so a handful of parser nodes. Monitor pages/s, frontier depth, the number of hosts currently eligible, and DNS latency. If throughput drops while fetchers are idle, the frontier is starved of ready hosts (add seeds or widen scope), not short of machines.

## What interviewers look for

- **Mid-level:** a correct loop (frontier, fetch, store, parse, enqueue), robots.txt compliance, URL dedupe and a blob store for content, with sensible timeouts.
- **Senior:** turns "be polite" into a concrete frontier design (per-host queues with a ready-time heap), sizes the fleet from the deadline, explains Bloom filter sizing and its false-positive trade-off, separates fetch and parse, and designs crash recovery with idempotent writes.
- **Staff:** reasons about crawl economics (priority, budgets per host, recrawl freshness), the hidden bottlenecks (DNS, shared-hosting IPs, ready-host starvation), operational signals and how the system evolves into a continuous recrawler.

## Common mistakes

- Treating the frontier as a single FIFO queue and adding politeness as an afterthought.
- Sharding the frontier by URL hash, which spreads one host over many shards and makes politeness a distributed coordination problem.
- Storing page bodies in a relational database.
- Ignoring DNS until the resolver becomes the bottleneck.
- Claiming exactly-once fetching instead of making writes idempotent.
- No defence against spider traps, giant responses or hosts that never respond.

## Self-review checklist

- [ ] The throughput target was converted to pages/s and concurrent connections.
- [ ] Politeness is enforced structurally (per-host queues sharded by host), including shared IPs.
- [ ] robots.txt is cached per host with a TTL and defined failure behaviour.
- [ ] URL dedupe uses normalisation plus a sized Bloom filter, and the false-positive trade-off is stated.
- [ ] Exact and near-duplicate content detection are distinguished.
- [ ] A node crash recovers from checkpoints, and replays are idempotent.
- [ ] Timeouts, size caps, depth limits and trap heuristics are present.

## Further reading

- [RFC 9309: Robots Exclusion Protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309)
- [Google Search Central: Introduction to robots.txt](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro)
- [Manku, Jain and Das Sarma: Detecting Near-Duplicates for Web Crawling](https://research.google/pubs/detecting-near-duplicates-for-web-crawling/)
keyTakeaways: Convert the deadline into pages per second and concurrent connections first; fetching is I/O-bound and cheap, scheduling is the hard part.
Politeness is a frontier design problem: per-host back queues with a next-eligible-time heap, sharded by host so no cross-node coordination is needed.
Cache robots.txt and DNS per host, define behaviour when robots.txt is unreachable, and rate-limit by IP as well as host name.
Normalise URLs, then use a sized Bloom filter for the seen set; use exact hashes plus SimHash for duplicate content.
Survive a multi-day run with leased frontier shards, periodic checkpoints and idempotent writes keyed by URL hash.
